strengths: Novel perspective on leveraging function decomposability in distributional optimization with elegant connection to message-passing algorithms
Rigorous mathematical development with multiple derivations (A.3, A.4) providing theoretical depth and robust value function bounds
Comprehensive experimental validation including synthetic benchmarks with exact decompositions and diverse protein design datasets with ablations
Clear algorithmic specification (Algorithm 1) with detailed implementation and promised code availability supporting reproducibility
Practical applicability demonstrated through systematic procedure for deriving decompositions from AlphaFold3 structures
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation inadequately addressed: method requires knowing a good decomposition a priori, but decomposition discovery process is minimally explored; Figure A5 demonstrates high sensitivity to decomposition parameters

Limited baseline comparisons: only naive EDA evaluated; missing comparisons to Factorized Distribution Algorithm, Bayesian optimization methods, and other decomposition-aware approaches mentioned in related work

Mixed empirical results: protein experiments show improvement in 3/4 datasets with TDP-43 showing no difference; improvements are modest (20-40% faster convergence) and diminish with larger sampling budgets (K=1000), questioning practical significance
No theoretical convergence analysis, sample complexity bounds, or characterization of when/why DADO helps; value function bound (Eq. 10) is loose with gap not characterized

Experimental design concerns: per-function hyperparameter sweeps risk unfair comparison; limited protein benchmark (4 main proteins) with one (Gcn4) failing due to invalid decomposition for intrinsically disordered proteins

Scope limitations: method fundamentally depends on decomposition quality but generality to non-protein domains (circuits, materials) is claimed but unvalidated; entire evaluation restricted to discrete amino acids

Algorithm sensitivity to multiple hyperparameters (learning rate η, temperature β, shaping function W, contact threshold t) requiring domain-specific tuning; single gradient step choice justified weakly

strengths: Sound theoretical framework connecting classical message-passing to distributional optimization with principled derivation of distributional value functions
Clear presentation building intuition from fully-decomposable to soft-decomposable settings with good use of examples
Comprehensive experiments including both synthetic and protein-based validation with thoughtful ablations on sample budget and decomposition thresholds
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes (e.g., TDP-43 showing no benefit, Gcn4 failure for disordered proteins)
Reproducibility practices including promised code release and detailed implementation specifications
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines classical message-passing (known for decades) with standard EDA; incremental over prior FDA work

Critical missing baselines: no comparisons to Factorized Distribution Algorithm (FDA), Bayesian Optimization methods, or other decomposition-aware approaches; unclear whether improvements come from decomposition awareness or other factors

Decomposition acquisition remains largely unsolved: threshold selection for proteins is highly sensitive (Fig. A5) with no principled method; fails for structurally dynamic proteins; vague guidance for other domains (circuits, materials)

Inconsistent protein results undermining practical claims: TDP-43 shows no benefit at K=1000 despite being longest; GB1 shows high variance late in training; benefits range from negligible to 2× across different proteins

No computational cost analysis: message-passing overhead for Q-function computation not quantified; wall-clock runtime comparisons absent despite potential significance on small problems (K=100, L=50)

Incomplete experimental validation: different hyperparameter sweep ranges for synthetic vs. protein experiments could introduce bias; initialization on low-scoring sequences adds confound; convergence criteria fixed arbitrarily at 100 iterations

Technical gaps: lower-bound tightness (Eq. 10) in practice unexplored; Q-function validity window sensitivity to gradient steps not ablated; no convergence rate analysis; shaping function W chosen without principled guidance

Unresolved practical deployment questions: How to select decompositions in domains without structural priors? What level of decomposition is necessary? How robust are results to decomposition misspecification?

strengths: Novel theoretical framework elegantly connecting classical message-passing to distributional optimization with rigorous mathematical development and proper lower bounds on value functions
Clear problem motivation with effective pedagogical progression from fully- to soft-decomposable cases; Figure 1 effectively communicates key insights
Comprehensive synthetic experiments convincingly demonstrate benefits of decomposition awareness across varying problem sizes (L=25-200, D=20)
Real-world applicability demonstrated on multiple protein datasets (7 total) with proper statistical testing and ablation studies on sample complexity
Strong reproducibility: code availability, detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, thorough supplementary materials with protocol details
weaknesses: Mixed real-world results undermine main claims: TDP-43 shows no improvement despite longest sequence; GB1 shows marginal significance (P=8.75e-05) with overlapping CIs; Gcn4 case explicitly fails; only 3/7 proteins show clear improvement at K=1000

Decomposition specification is non-trivial and critical: performance depends heavily on contact threshold (e.g., t=4.5Å shows no benefit, but t=2.75Å does); no principled guidance for threshold selection or decomposition in other domains despite claims of generality
Limited experimental scope: all real experiments on proteins only; zero experiments on circuits, telescopes, or materials despite being mentioned as applications; makes generalizability unclear

Insufficient comparison with related work: FDA never empirically compared; no comparison with Bayesian Optimization methods exploiting structure; only compared against naive EDA; no ablation separating message-passing from factorization
Missing scalability analysis: no runtime comparisons, computational complexity analysis, or experiments on large design spaces (L>118); message-passing overhead on deep junction trees not discussed

Hyperparameter tuning potentially unfair: learning rate and temperature optimized separately for each method/problem; no sensitivity analysis provided; unclear if improvements are algorithmic or tuning artifacts
Statistical concerns: multiple comparisons across 7+ proteins without correction; wide confidence intervals in several cases make practical significance unclear relative to uncertainty

Model misspecification underexplored: interaction between inaccurate learned decompositions and DADO performance not analyzed; no investigation of whether poor decomposition could hurt DADO more than baseline

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing a real problem in scientific design where many objectives naturally decompose across design variables
Rigorous theoretical development with principled derivation connecting classical message-passing to distributional optimization, including multiple perspectives and formal proofs

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including systematic synthetic experiments across problem complexities, multiple real protein datasets, proper statistical testing with confidence intervals, and robustness analyses
Consistent improvements across all tested problems compared to appropriate baselines (naive EDA, FDA) in both synthetic and real settings
Strong reproducibility: code available on GitHub, detailed hyperparameters, complete dataset documentation, and experimental setup
Clear presentation with informative figures and well-organized appendices providing thorough technical details
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily applies existing EDA and message-passing frameworks to the decomposition-aware setting; no convergence analysis or optimality guarantees specific to DADO

Strong dependency on known decomposition structure; Figure A6-A7 reveals significant sensitivity to decomposition specification (contact threshold), undermining practical applicability without guidance on determining decomposability in new domains

Modest experimental improvements: overlapping confidence intervals with FDA baseline in several cases; no comparison with other structure-exploiting discrete optimization methods or Bayesian optimization variants

Limited scope of real experiments: only protein property prediction tested; scalability to longer sequences (L > 84) or larger alphabets (D > 21) remains unclear; no demonstration on other scientific design domains
Incomplete analysis of design choices: why synthetic performance gap decreases with L while real improvements persist; limited discussion of failure modes or misspecified decomposition sensitivity
Runtime gains are modest (1-2x) and appear due to sampling efficiency rather than wall-clock improvements; computational complexity analysis is missing

Dense mathematical notation in Sec. 2.1 could be simplified; critical details about decomposition sensitivity buried in appendices; entropy-maximizing variant (A.5) feels disconnected and underdeveloped
All synthetic experiments use similar random junction tree structures; testing on diverse structure types would strengthen claims about generalization

strengths: Mathematically rigorous framework connecting classical message-passing to distributional optimization with detailed derivations and formal justifications
Comprehensive experimental scope spanning synthetic functions with varying complexity and multiple real protein design problems
Novel and well-motivated application to protein design using AlphaFold3-predicted structure to discover function decomposition
Detailed algorithmic exposition (Algorithm 1) with transparent implementation details and promised code availability
Extensive robustness analyses including sensitivity to graph mutations and threshold variations
weaknesses: Core algorithmic novelty is limited - applying EDA with factorized distributions based on known decompositions is straightforward; similar ideas (factorized distributions, message-passing) are well-established in Bayesian optimization and graphical models

Critical practical limitation: method requires expensive prior decomposition discovery (running AlphaFold3, pre-training on 1,000 sequences, threshold selection), with computational cost underacknowledged and not fully factored into runtime comparisons

Empirical improvements on real protein design problems are modest and often statistically marginal (Amyloid p=1.39e-05, Gen4 p=2.53e-06 with overlapping confidence intervals; AAV2 shows DADO is slower: 2.1 vs 3.4 min)

Experimental design heavily biased toward DADO: synthetic experiments use functions with ideal decomposition structures rarely seen in practice; baselines are weak (naive EDA, 1999 FDA, PPO) with missing comparisons to modern discrete optimization and recent protein design methods
Limited theoretical contribution: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or analysis of decomposition misspecification effects; no characterization of when DADO outperforms naive EDA
Insufficient practical guidance on when practitioners should use DADO versus simpler alternatives; unclear whether modest empirical gains justify added complexity for real protein design applications
Unclear computational efficiency: Table 1 shows only modest speedups that don't clearly justify complexity; message-passing efficiency claims not convincingly supported by runtime analysis

Limited validation scale: only 4 proteins tested with non-uniform success; extensive sensitivity analysis (A.9.4-A.9.6) reveals significant performance degradation with threshold changes, questioning decomposition robustness
